items.title: The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently
items.summary: “There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them because it’s sort of obvious.” Last week, I spoke with Jimmy Wales — the man responsible for Wikipedia, the darling of students all over the world since 2001. Our conversation meandered pleasantly over philosophy, technology, cryptocurrency, politics, history, and more. (Big Think members can get first access to watch the full video at this link.) But Wales’s fish parable hit me. What “water” do I swim in? Of course, you can take this two ways. First, the water can be seen broadly: the slightly opaque “ways of thinking” we operate under in the 21st-century post-Enlightenment West. We’ll park that discussion for another day . But we can also see this “water” more practically: What specific facts or pieces of information do I think I know, but aren’t as “obvious” as I thought? I feel as if it’s my philosophical duty to raise doubts where no doubts existed before. And so, here are five “facts” that are actually far more disputed in life — and on Wikipedia — than you might have thought. 1. The Wright brothers invented the airplane Of course! If you’re feeling really bookish, you could add “Kitty Hawk, December 1903.” The story of the Wright brothers is such a Hollywood-ready fact that it’s almost impossible to forget: two bicycle makers, one windy beach, and twelve seconds in the air. Unless you went to school in Brazil. Brazilians have two objections to the Wright brothers’ claim: First, no official watched their 1903 flight. Second, the Wright Flyer needed a rail to take off. So, Brazilians give credit for the airplane’s invention to Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew his 14-bis biplane near Paris in the autumn of 1906. He did so in public with Aéro-Club officials on hand to measure it, and he took off on his own wheels. Wikipedia doesn’t come down on either side. It has a whole article for the rival claims, where the Wrights and Santos-Dumont have to share the page with Gustave Whitehead, Samuel Langley, and a few other men who were absolutely, definitely first. 2. Alan Turing cracked the Enigma code In 2021, I wrote my book Mini Philosophy , and it was published with three mistakes. First, I wrongly claimed Christopher Nolan directed The Joker . (It was Todd Phillips.) Second, I attributed a quote to Aristotle that actually came from a scholar of Aristotle. But the third mistake, by far and away, was the one that caused the most uproar. I got emails, letters, and pretty intense direct messages. I had claimed the British had cracked the Enigma code. It was Alan Turing and the geniuses of Bletchley Park, surely? That’s what I’d grown up with. But Enigma was first broken in Warsaw at the end of 1932 by a 27-year-old Polish mathematician named Marian Rejewski. That’s almost seven years before the war began. He and his colleagues, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, spent the 1930s reading German messages. Then, in late July 1939 — five weeks before the invasion of Poland — they invited British and French codebreakers to a forest outside Warsaw and showed them how it was done. None of this is a secret. Rejewski’s Wikipedia page sums up what he is known for in a single line: “Solving the Enigma machine cipher.” And GCHQ’s own history is happy to say that the first British Bombe owed a great deal to Turing’s meeting with Polish codebreakers. Turing was still a genius, but he was also standing on Polish shoulders. I mean, really, this fact isn’t so much “disputed” as just “Jonny, you were wrong.” 3. There are seven continents I kind of knew all the other facts on this list before researching this article, but this one was a shock. Seven. There are seven continents. I admit there’s a bit of controversy around “Australia” vs. “Australasia” vs. “Oceania,” but we all agree on seven, right? But in Greece and much of the Romance-speaking world, from Lisbon to Lima, children learn that there are six continents, because North and South America are a single continent called “America.” Russian children learn six as well, but a different six: The Americas stay apart, but Europe and Asia are merged into Eurasia. Something a lot of anthropologists and geologists do as well. And the Olympic flag has five rings for five inhabited continents — one America again, with Antarctica left off altogether until the penguins whip together a bobsled team. The Wikipedia article doesn’t pick a winner. There are, it says, up to seven continents and as few as four. Which means that somewhere, right now, two perfectly well-educated adults are arguing in a pub about something they each learned before they could tie their shoelaces. And they’re both right. 4. The United States won the War of 1812 That depends on who you ask, and in this case, there are three people you could ask. Ask a Canadian, and you’ll hear about a plucky Canada seeing off an American invasion. Ask an American, and it’s the “Second War of American Independence.” Ask a Brit, and you’ll mostly get a blank look because, for Britain, it was a sideshow to the real business of beating Napoleon. And we’ve loved to hate the French ever since. In a 2009 poll, 37% of Canadians said Canada won, and only 9% gave it to the United States. Not every American would argue. “By my count,” the American historian Donald Hickey said, “we lost the War of 1812, and we lost Vietnam.” And Wikipedia? Its editors have spent years on the question. There is a dedicated discussion page titled “Who Won?” and then there was a formal mediation case. And after all that, the article settles on calling the entire debate “inconclusive.” 5. The Second World War began in 1939 On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. “This country is at war with Germany,” the British Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, said at the time. And so, that’s when the Second World War started. But in Russia, the war that matters — the “Great Patriotic War” — began on June 22, 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In China, it starts much earlier. In 2017, the Ministry of Education announced that the war against Japan would be counted from 1931, not 1937, and an 8-year war became a 14-year war overnight. Wikipedia keeps a whole archive of editors arguing about this, and at one point, the article itself cited 1937 as the start. My favorite contribution comes from an editor who backed 1939 on entirely practical grounds: They said that if Wikipedia said 1937, a teenager somewhere would copy it into their homework and be marked wrong. Which is, I think, the whole point. So often, the “right” answer is simply the one your teacher is expecting. But both the teacher and the student are stuck in the same problem. As Georg Hegel, Jimmy Wales, and Pink Floyd all knew, we are all just fish swimming in a fishbowl, and no one’s commenting on the water. This article The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently is featured on Big Think .

items.title: What Could Replace the Trump Style of Politics?
items.summary: J onathan Spector’s play Birthright , which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel. In the last act, which takes place in 2024, the nearly two-decade bond between a group of American Jewish friends has frayed over Gaza. Izzy, the most left-wing of the bunch, has already abandoned their online group chat, where the friends shared photos of their newborn children, checked in during COVID, and planned their reunions. Thrown together for a funeral, Izzy and another friend, Chaya, begin to argue—as one does these days—about Zionism. They quickly whip out their phones, mustering evidence. “Theodor Herzl colonialism,” Izzy types into the search window, which—in an ingenious bit of stagecraft—appears projected on the wall behind her and starts to flow with online sources. “1930s partition plan Israel,” Chaya counter-Googles. They start scrolling through newspaper articles and Wikipedia pages, hurling raw historical information at each other like malfunctioning robots. But no one is listening. Their friend Noah, watching from the side, offers that going to the internet to prove your point is useless because you’ll invariably find what you’re looking for—“which is why I think this is really, really not a good way to go about having an actual conversation.” This mode of political discourse is surely familiar: the search for a truth that will detonate like an atom bomb, ripping the roof off every other truth. Most of us know that this outcome never, ever happens. But beneath the awareness of information bubbles and fake news, of epistemic breakdown, lies a stubbornly common belief that total victory is achievable. This fantasy has even become its own kind of entertainment—think of Jubilee Media ’s viral videos in which one person has to fend off 20 political opponents like a medieval knight, or the late Charlie Kirk ’s “Prove Me Wrong” college tours. Theories are packed tight with facts and lobbed back and forth in what the German philosopher Hannah Arendt once called “an orgy of truth-telling.” Arendt used this strange phrase in a 1946 letter to the philosopher Gershom Scholem, her dear intellectual sparring partner, after they had gotten into a fierce argument about—what else?—Zionism. One shouldn’t be a “fanatic for truth,” Arendt told him. All this did was harden people in their positions: I have my truth, you have yours, and the only way forward is for you to admit that not just your opinions but your facts are wrong . This is no way to hold a debate, or to conduct politics; all it does is create stasis or even worse. Elsewhere, Arendt called truth in this context “despotic.” She argued instead for a different mode, one that would be surprising—okay, maybe fantastical—to consider today: “an orgy of friendship.” In a recently published book, A World We Share , Roger Berkowitz explores the German philosopher’s thoughts on friendship “as the lens through which she understood politics.” For Arendt, who is best known for her hard-bitten analysis of totalitarianism, friendship might seem to be an uncharacteristically schmaltzy subject, but as filtered through her mind, abstracted and held apart, it sheds all Hallmark associations. Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center for Politics and Humanities at Bard College, provides the material for an intriguing thought experiment, one that might be useful as Americans rub their eyes in the post-midterms dawn. After a decade in which Donald Trump’s tribalist instincts have only accelerated that rush to Google-dueling, it might be worth pursuing Arendt’s idea that friendship, as opposed to truth-telling, is a better model for conducting politics. A rendt never left behind a treatise on friendship, but references to the concept pop up throughout her work and letters. Berkowitz, who has a granular familiarity with her writing, brings all of the strands together. For Arendt, friendship is distinct from love as we often think of it; it is not about losing yourself in order to meld with another person and separate from the rest of the world. Instead, this kind of connection preserves difference and feeds off plurality. Friendship is actually the most worldly of relationships because it forces us to accommodate the separateness of the people we know and care about. [ Read: It’s the morality, stupid ] Arendt articulated three defining features: time spent knowing each other (“a two-week-old friendship does not exist,” she said); talking and more talking and even more talking; and a respect and appreciation for the unique conditions that shape someone else’s worldview. This kind of friendship, she thought, should withstand even the most violent disagreements. “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions,” she wrote in her letter to Scholem, begging that they not lose their connection despite her public disillusionment with the idea of an exclusively Jewish state—a critique Scholem must have felt as a body blow. Berkowitz points out that for Arendt, what makes us human “is not our ability to reason or our grasp of moral certainty or absolute truth but our ability to form lasting and meaningful relationships grounded in mutual recognition and respect.” The fact that she and Scholem had spent more than a decade talking, listening, and yelling was more important to her than any need for them to come to similar conclusions. Her emphasis was rather on this “in-between,” the “common world” they shared and built just by continuing to engage on the issues that mattered to them both. Could any of this possibly be applicable to America’s political culture, which most days resembles the fear and loathing of trench warfare? Dream with me for a minute. Imagine if arguments at Thanksgiving dinner or in Congress proceeded with an awareness that conquering the other person’s worldview was impossible—in the way you can’t really change that old friend who keeps dating the wrong people. Imagine if the goal was to tease out commonalities, instead of trying to will the differences away. This type of politics would be fueled by persuasion, as opposed to force or truth, Berkowitz writes; it would aim “neither at domination nor certainty. It is not about being right.” Arendt’s favored metaphor for this in-between is a table around which people with disparate views and interests sit. The existence of the table matters more than anyone’s particular opinions. The American version of this table does exist, however alienated we may feel from one another. The changing state of the economy, for example, or the future of children’s education, are issues that could potentially be served at this table. Some topics—say, abortion rights—would produce more heat, maybe some fist-pounding. But if the objective is to make sure that the table itself doesn’t evaporate, the conversation might continue. Certain shared worries from our shared world will present themselves as commonalities, even as people’s perspectives remain distinct. Take the proliferation of data centers or the cost of health care. “By talking about what is between them,” Arendt writes, friends and citizens can make that shared world “ever more common.” [ Read: Why we should read Hannah Arendt now ] This is what an orgy of friendship (as opposed to one of truth) could look like. I don’t have any illusions that this shift of mindset is easy. But some politicians could point the way—for instance Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas. “I really do believe that the key to saving the American experiment is loving our enemies,” he recently told Michelle Goldberg at The New York Times . “How do we love each other through our disagreements? How do we remember each other’s humanity? How do we handle each other with more care?” Talarico gives this a Christian gloss with his talk of “love,” which is not quite what Arendt had in mind, but she would otherwise be sympathetic to his willingness to make friends with those who have been calling him

items.title: I Share a Closet With His Emotional Baggage
items.summary: How to Live Rent-Free in Someone’s Head I took Jacob up on his offer. Yes, it was soon-ish to make such a big move—just a month and change since we got together officially—but we’d known each other for longer, and I felt like it could be something real. My lease was up. He said there was space. My sister was being dramatic about how I would lose my identity and become nothing more than the idea of me in his mind . But honestly, the bigger thing I was worried about was Marnie. I was not made aware that Marnie would be there. That first day, I walked in and found her stretched out on the futon, painting her toenails green. “Hi!” she said. “You must be Jill. Jacob’s told me so much about you.” Obviously I knew who Marnie was. I was probably the world’s living expert on Marnie after all the time I spent listening to Jacob cry about her, back before he and I got together. “Is that all you brought?” She pointed to my garbage bag. I twisted my hands through the pull strings. Most of my things were in storage in my sister’s basement. “It’s just temporary,” I said. “Until we can get a real place.” Then Marnie offered to help me unpack, which, no. I had been looking forward to that part, the taking things out of the bag and putting them in places, that new-drawer feeling. But there was no drawer. Jacob had said he would clear one out for me, but every drawer I opened was full of random stuff, clothes and socks and stacks of receipts but also a conch shell, a box full of plastic straws, a sewing kit, a saxophone—and of course I started to wonder if all of this stuff was Jacob’s or if some of it was Marnie’s. It was like a regular apartment. Except it had no windows and too many doors, most of them locked, and the unlocked ones opening into closets packed with junk that fell on you if you opened them. It’ll be just like having our own place , he’d said, and it sort of was, except most of the time he wasn’t there. It smelled like him, and I remembered all the times I had lain awake in my old apartment wishing I could be there. But at odd moments I’d be brushing my teeth or sweeping the floor and Marnie would walk by, crunching her way through a giant bag of crackers. Also I was pretty sure she was using my shampoo. “I’m not,” said Marnie. “You’re using my shampoo.” I pulled a chunk of my hair to my nose and sniffed it. You might wonder why I’d bother washing my hair there. But I always thought Jacob might come in at any second. When he was there, there were things like a kitchen table and a TV and a bed, things that made it feel like home. He almost never came in during the day, though, even though to me the whole benefit of our situation was that theoretically he could check in anytime. Hey babe what time are you — “He’s not coming,” said Marnie. “It’s game night.” She pulled out her guitar and started singing the same song, over and over and over. When he was there, though, it was so great. One night he came in full of all this energy and curled his arms around me, burrowed his head into my shoulder. ”I don’t know how you put up with this place. God, what a mess.” He clomped around, pulling open all the closets and opening boxes of stuff. He dumped things out on the futon: a winter coat, a fondue maker with two little silver sticks. He wanted to make space for me, to give me the kind of place I deserved. “Check these out!” He spread baseball cards on the floor. “I haven’t looked at these in ages. I bet some of them are worth a lot.” He formed stacks, then shuffled them all together and formed different stacks. “He’s not going to clean it up, you know,” said Marnie, hours later. She sat cross-legged in a nest of flannel green plaid camping blankets. I couldn’t see the futon or any of the furniture. Jacob was gone for the night. “Maybe I could just start with some of the big things.” I pulled an empty box and started putting things in it. Old sporting equipment, school papers, a guitar. I wrote “high school” on a label. Marnie watched from her nest. “You could help,” I said. “Why would I do that?” “Maybe because you live here too?” “You should leave it. It’s his crap.” She sounded like my sister. “I’m his girlfriend. A good girlfriend.” I tried to pull another box down and sent a cascade of stuff tumbling down over the box I’d just packed. Marnie snorted. “What are you even doing here?” I said. “No one wants you.” “Ouch. I’m devastated.” She took a long slurp of Diet Coke. I made a lot of progress over the next few days. Or, I think they were days. I didn’t like to admit it, but if Jacob forgot to check in after work, it was hard to tell one day from another. But it was nice to have a project, a purpose. And that weekend, Jacob and I had plans to spend some quality time together, just us. I straightened a stack of books, fluffed a bunch of silk flowers I’d found scattered among some old vintage dresses. “Sorry I’m late, babe. I don’t know why you put up with me.” I jumped up and wrapped my arms around him. The way he smelled, the laundry soap and the buzz of his voice against my chest. It felt real. We were going to spend the evening just watching bad TV in a clean room and maybe we could talk about the future, about us. “Hey,” he said, “where are my baseball cards?” He tore through box after box. “Why would you do this? I didn’t say you could touch my stuff!” “I was trying to help.” I picked at a strand of my hair, the ends split and split again. “Marnie left it really messy.” “Marnie? What are you talking about?” He dumped boxes one by one, strewing items across the floor. “Marnie doesn’t live here.” A stack of boxes fell over and Marnie was there, doubled over, coughing. “Yes, she does,” I said. “She’s literally right there.” “Wow.” He stopped dumping boxes for a second and just stared at me. “I thought you were more mature than this.” I crawled into a little space next to the futon and covered my face. I could hear Jacob shuffling around the room, ripping open boxes. For the first time in a long time, I thought about leaving. Not leaving leaving, just getting some space. I could crash on my sister’s couch for a while, just until I found a real place. Marnie was right next to me, breathing. “Why are you even here?” I said. She took a sip from a water bottle covered in faded stickers. “Honestly, I’m not sure. I had everything packed at one point. But there’s no door. They all just lead to closets.” I dug my knuckles into my eyes. My breath hiccuped in my throat. “Ugh,” said Marnie. “Here.” She wrapped her green camping blanket around my shoulders. Her hair smelled like apples. A while later Jacob crawled in next to me. Marnie scooted over. “I’m sorry,” he said into my hair. “I know I’m the worst.” “It’s fine.” “Shoot. You’re mad.” “I’m not mad.” He wrapped his arms around me. “This is what I love about you, Jill. You’re so chill.” I was mad, and then, like that, I wasn’t. I was chill, just like he said. On the floor around us, his baseball cards were all lined up, tiny faces looking at me in the dark. It wasn’t that messy, really. It was probably all in my head. items.title: Voyager’s cosmic map of Earth’s location: Cute, but wrong
items.summary: Here in late 2026, an incredible milestone has been reached: the Voyager 1 spacecraft — humanity’s most distant spacecraft from Earth — has finally passed a distance of one light-day from us. Along with its twin, Voyager 2, these two spacecraft have left the confines of the Solar System and now traverse interstellar space, freely floating through the interstellar medium. Eventually, their radioactive sources will decay away enough that they’ll become entirely inoperable, but there’s a chance that someday, in the far future, an alien species will encounter and recover one or both of these ancient artifacts: humanity’s first foray into the Universe beyond our own Solar System. Aboard each of these two Voyagers is a special message intended for anyone who’d find them, whether in the near or distant future: the Voyager golden record . Containing songs, images, and sounds of Earth, it was designed to be an information-laden cosmic time capsule, capable of being easily deciphered by any intelligent alien species to come upon it. It was meant as an introduction to Earth and humanity, with the vision of serving as a cultural ambassador for our planet. Emblazoned on the cover of the record are a series of diagrams , including one that we thought was incredibly important at the time: a map of Earth’s location in the galaxy, as determined through the mapping of 14 radio-loud pulsars. Although the method used to locate Earth was, for its time, a very clever one, we now understand that it’s inherently flawed. Anyone who receives it will most likely be unable to track down where our planet is from the included information, making it a cute, but wrongheaded, artifact from our cosmic infancy. This color-coded version of the pulsar map to the 14 pulsars chosen for the Voyager golden records displays their relative distances and pulse timing periods to 12 significant figures, with the fastest included pulsar taking right around 30 milliseconds to complete a full 360 degree rotation but the slowest rotators taking more than a second to do so. The pulsars can be seen to occupy different directions in space at different distances. Credit : Sam W/Simple Desktops The whole point of the golden record was that it would serve as sort of a “time capsule” of humanity and Earth: an attempt to reach out to whomever might be out there in the Universe and share with them a little bit about what our world is like and what humanity — at its best — is all about. Carl Sagan, cocreator of the golden record, put it as follows: “We [are] a species endowed with hope and perseverance, at least a little intelligence, substantial generosity and a palpable zest to make contact with the cosmos.” Today, despite our stumbles and missteps in the 49 years that have ensued since the launch of the dual Voyager spacecraft, all of these things remain true. At the time, pulsars were a relatively new discovery. The very first one had only been discovered back in 1967, when then-graduate student Jocelyn Bell (later Jocelyn Bell Burnell ), while surveying the sky for quasars, instead found a surprising signal on her chart-recorder papers that she described as a “bit of scruff.” After digging into that signal, she found that it was a radio emitter that pulsed with great regularity. Initially named LGM-1, for “Little Green Man 1,” it was soon determined not to be a signal of alien origin at all, but rather a rapidly rotating neutron star that emitted radio pulses. Today, that neutron star is known as our first pulsar, and has the less-poetic name PSR B1919+21 . This image shows Jocelyn Bell (now Jocelyn Bell Burnell) at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory alongside the telescope used to collect the data in which she identified the first known pulsar: a bright, regular radio source that is now known to correspond to a highly magnetized, rapidly spinning neutron star. This photo was taken one year later in 1968. Credit : Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory Bell Burnell herself was the one who showed that this was unlikely to be a signal from intelligent extraterrestrials, when she continued her work and found a similar signal originating from a different part of the sky. Thomas Gold suggested the origin of pulsars should be rapidly rotating neutron stars the year after they were first discovered, in 1968. Originally discovered in the radio band, pulsars were swiftly detected over a wide variety of wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum. The first optical pulsar was discovered in January of 1969, and in May of 1969 the first X-ray pulsar was discovered in the heart of the Crab Nebula: a pulsar that was known to emit radio waves since the year prior. By the time the Voyager spacecraft were launched in 1977, there were a cumulative 149 pulsars that had been discovered, and pulsar evolution had also been detected. In late 1968, the Crab pulsar’s period was found to slowly increase, meaning that the pulsar was spinning down over time. In 1969, the first “glitch” in a pulsar system was detected: an instantaneous change in the pulse period of a pulsar. Pulse period decay was identified in many more pulsars, and as of 1977, the period of the known pulsars ranged from a little over 1 second to as fast as 33 pulses per second. This computer simulation of a neutron star shows charged particles being whipped around by a neutron star’s extraordinarily strong electric and magnetic fields. It is possible that a neutron star has formed within the remnant of SN 1987A, but the region is still too dusty and gas-rich for the “pulses” to seep out. Neutron star surfaces are at similar temperatures to white dwarf interiors: typically at several hundred thousand kelvin. Credit : NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center We also had a rudimentary picture — just ten years after their initial discovery — for how these pulsars worked. The idea was that a neutron star was spinning, and that a neutron star itself isn’t just a ball of neutrons, but rather is a core of dense neutrons surrounded by a thin shell of atomic nuclei, including a mix of protons and neutrons combined, and much lighter electrons as well. As the neutron star spins, the much heavier protons and the much lighter electrons separate, and wind up with slightly different distributions across the neutron star’s outer layers and surface. Whenever you have a set of electric charges in motion, they’re going to produce a magnetic field. The more charges you have, the greater a charge separation you have, the greater the charge density you have, and the faster the charges move, the stronger the generated magnetic field will be. Whereas the Earth has a magnetic field of about 1 Gauss, the strongest permanent magnets we can generate have a field strength of around 14,000 Gauss, and the strongest laboratory electromagnets have a magnitude of around 300,000-500,000 Gauss, the strength of a rotating neutron star’s magnetic field can routinely reach or exceed 100 trillion Gauss (10 Gauss): incredibly strong magnetic fields. The idea is that these fields then accelerate material, such as electrons, around them, and the accelerated material produces “blips” of radiation each time the pulsar completes one revolution. This image shows the illustration of a massive neutron star, along with the distorted gravitational effects an observer might see if they had the capability of viewing this neutron star at such a close distance. While neutron stars are famous for pulsing, not every neutron star is a pulsar. The fastest pulsars, known as millisecond pulsars, rotate at more than 100 times per second, with the current record holder completing a whopping 766 rotations each second.
